finding: Test 18 still reads 'Each delta predicate is measured against the unit's baseline file, and a spec, HEAD or task count unchanged since spawn fails the predicate.' Round 4's new disjunctions in §3.3 make that false for two kinds: an unchanged spec no longer fails `review-resolve` (every finding resolved also passes), and an unchanged HEAD no longer fails `audit-fix` (a finding recorded resolved without a change also passes). The repair changed the rule and left the test asserting the pre-repair rule, so implementation would have to violate one of the two.
suggestion: Rewrite test 18 to enumerate per kind: unchanged spec/HEAD/task-count fails for the kinds whose predicate is a pure delta, and for `review-resolve`/`audit-fix` assert both branches explicitly — unchanged-and-still-unresolved fails, unchanged-and-newly-resolved passes.

finding: TP_RUN_DIR is .tp/runs/$TP_RUN_ID with a fresh ULID per run, and TP_ROUND_DIR is $TP_RUN_DIR/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND. If a run dies mid-round after three of five role units wrote their files, the next run gets a NEW run id, so its round directory is empty; the record unit merges '$TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson' (§6.3) and therefore merges only the roles the second run happened to re-execute. That directly contradicts §10.1 test 6 ('a crashed driver loses nothing') and makes an undercounted round recordable — exactly the defect §8a's dropped-role rule exists to prevent. The spec never says whether the second run re-runs every role for the round, adopts the previous run's round directory, or how the oracle decides which roles are still pending.
suggestion: Anchor the round directory to the cycle rather than the run (e.g. .tp/rounds/<phase>-r<round>/, with TP_RUN_DIR keeping only run-scoped artifacts), or state explicitly that a resumed run re-executes every role of an incomplete round and that pre-existing files for that round are discarded first. Either way say how next_units decides which role units of a partially completed round are still pending.

finding: Round 4 changed TP_RUNNER from 'the env layer of the existing precedence, so no new precedence rule is introduced' to 'a test-only override that outranks every layer of §7's precedence, including a CLI flag'. §7 was not updated and still states the fields resolve through 'CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in'; `runner` is one of those fields. §10.2 test 16 likewise still asserts, for each §7 field, that 'a CLI flag beats a task override' with no exception for the runner. The spec now carries two incompatible precedence rules for the same field.
suggestion: State the exception in §7 itself (an explicit TP_RUNNER > CLI row for `runner`, with the test-seam rationale) and amend test 16 to assert it, or revert TP_RUNNER to the env layer and give the test its own mechanism (e.g. a test-only build tag or a `--runner` flag the test passes) rather than an out-of-band precedence.

finding: The `audit-fix` unit's id is 'the finding index' (§3.1) and its durable write is 'HEAD differs from head_sha, or the finding is recorded resolved without a change'. Neither the index's ordering nor the resolution mechanism exists: there is no stated index over audit findings (which round's file? which sort? does it renumber as findings resolve?), and tp has no documented audit-side counterpart to `tp review --resolve` for a single finding, so neither the driver nor the Stop hook can evaluate 'the finding is recorded resolved'. Since (kind, id) is also the last_failure clearing key (§4.2), an index that shifts between rounds silently clears or strands failures for a different finding.
suggestion: Define a stable audit-finding identifier (e.g. round + role + item_id, the pair tp audit --merge already dedups on) and name the command that records one finding resolved, or drop `audit-fix` to a whole-round fix unit whose durable write is a HEAD change.

finding: The no-change disjunctions added to `review-resolve` ('or every finding is resolved') and `audit-fix` ('or the finding is recorded resolved without a change') are not measurable against the unit's baseline file, whose contents §3.1 fixes as {head_sha, spec_hash, task_count, round}. Nothing in the baseline records which findings were already resolved before the unit started, so the paragraph directly under the table — 'Each predicate is absolute or measured against the unit's baseline file, never against an unstated before' — no longer holds for two of the eight rows. Worse, both disjuncts are satisfied by a unit that did nothing: a `review-resolve` unit that crashes on a round whose findings were already resolved passes its own success test and passes the Stop hook (§6.2), which is exactly the do-nothing-succeeds hole the earlier rounds closed.
suggestion: Either add the resolution state to the baseline file (e.g. `unresolved_findings` count at spawn) and word the disjuncts as deltas against it — 'the unresolved-finding count is below the baseline's, or is zero and was zero at spawn only when …' — or drop the disjuncts and let a genuinely no-op unit be handled by the escalation record, which is already the spec's channel for 'nothing to do here'.

finding: Round 4 added the stop_reason precedence order and placed `converged` LAST, below every cap and `no-units`. That inverts §3.1 step 2 (releasable is checked first, before caps at step 6) and §4.1 (`tp run` exits 0 with stop_reason converged 'on that condition alone'). Under the new order a run whose final iteration makes the cycle releasable while the wall-clock or unit cap has also been reached records `cap-wall-clock`/`cap-units` and exits non-zero — the release signal §1 promises is lost, and an outer scheduler reading the exit code re-runs a finished cycle. A cap is a bound on the run; it cannot un-converge a releasable cycle.
suggestion: Move `converged` to the front of the precedence list (or immediately after `escalation`) and state the reason: convergence is an absolute property of the cycle, caps are properties of the run. Alternatively keep it last but then reconcile §3.1 step 2 and §4.1, which currently promise the opposite.

finding: The stop-reason precedence list ends `...cap-units, no-units, converged`, making `converged` lose to every cap when a checkpoint satisfies several rows. But §3.1's loop checks releasability at step 2 — before caps are checked at step 6 — so in the actual control flow `converged` always wins over a cap satisfied in the same iteration. The two orderings state opposite outcomes for the same situation (last unit of the cycle closes the work AND trips `cap-units`): §3.1 exits 0 converged, §3.4 records `cap-units`.
suggestion: Decide which holds and state it once. Either move `converged` to the head of §3.4's precedence list (matching the loop's step-2-first order), or change §3.1 to evaluate caps before releasability and say explicitly that a run which converges on its last permitted unit still reports the cap.

finding: 'A run with no stop_reason reports in_flight when the run lock is held and crashed when it is not' names two values but no field to carry them. stop_reason is null in both cases, and §3.4 lists the eight legal stop_reason values, none of which is in_flight or crashed. Test 14 and test 35 both assert this distinction, so both are unwritable until the JSON key (and whether the values are a new field or an overload of stop_reason) is pinned.
suggestion: Name the field and its domain explicitly, e.g. --status emits state: one of in_flight, crashed, stopped, and stop_reason stays null unless the run ended. Reference that field in tests 14 and 35.

finding: The run lock is per task file (`.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`, §3.1), so two `tp run` processes over different task files in one repo are explicitly permitted. But `.tp/run.json` (§3.5) and `.tp/last_failure.json` (§4.2) are single un-namespaced repo-level files, and `tp run --status` reads 'the current or last run' with no base selector. Two concurrent runs therefore overwrite each other's run state and last_failure, and --status cannot say which base it is describing — while §3.5 mandates atomic writes only for the sibling-unit case, not the concurrent-run case.
suggestion: Scope the state files to the base the lock is scoped to (e.g. `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`) and give `tp run --status` the same spec/--file argument as `tp run`; or state that at most one `tp run` may be active per repo and make the lock repo-scoped rather than base-scoped.

finding: The unattended fence covers `review_max_rounds`/`audit_max_rounds` but not the driver's own caps. §7 declares `run_max_units`, `run_max_wall_clock_seconds`, `run_max_budget_usd`, `run_max_unit_retries` as ordinary workflow fields resolving at read time through the same layered path, and §6.2's PreToolUse deny only stops hand-editing `.tp/config.json` — `tp set --workflow run_max_units=99999` is a supported route. That is exactly §5.1's own stated threat (an agent that raises its own budget and then declares convergence), applied to the caps that bound the run rather than the round.
suggestion: Either add the `run_*` cap fields to §5.1's fail-closed table (raising above the resolved value exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED), or state in §3.4 that the driver resolves its caps once at run start and ignores later changes for the life of the run — and say which, since 'resolves at read time' otherwise makes them mutable mid-run.

finding: 'an input whose lines all fail to parse makes --merge exit 1' does not define the zero-line case. A role that found nothing is instructed to write an empty (zero-byte) file, so on a clean round EVERY input has parsed=0. Implemented as `parsed == 0` the rule makes every clean round exit 1 and the run can never converge; implemented as `parsed == 0 && skipped > 0` it works. The implementer must guess which, and the two readings differ on the single most important round of the loop.
suggestion: State the predicate literally: an input exits 1 only when skipped > 0 and parsed == 0; a zero-line input is valid, reports {parsed:0, skipped:0}, and does not fail the merge. Add a test for a clean round of all-empty role files exiting 0.

finding: The dropped-role rule says an input whose lines all fail to parse makes --merge exit 1, but a zero-byte findings file is the documented way a role reports 'nothing found' (a clean role writes an empty file). With zero lines the predicate 'all lines fail to parse' is vacuously true, so one engineer writes a test asserting exit 1 for an empty role file and another asserts exit 0. Nothing in §8a or test 32 pins the empty-file case, and it is the case that decides whether a clean review round can ever merge.
suggestion: State the predicate over counts: --merge exits 1 only when an input has parsed==0 AND skipped>0; an input with parsed==0 and skipped==0 (empty file) is a legitimate clean role and exits 0. Add that empty-file case to test 32.

finding: The new 'A dropped role does not merge clean' rule says 'an input whose lines all fail to parse makes --merge exit 1'. A legitimately clean role produces a zero-line findings file — §3.3's `review-role`/`audit-role` durable write is only that the .ndjson *exists*, and the role prompts instruct an empty file when there is nothing real. For such a file parsed=0 and skipped=0, which reads as 'all lines failed to parse' under a vacuous quantifier, so the repair aimed at a dropped role can fail every clean round instead — the precise failure an unattended driver cannot recover from, and a re-run of the already-recorded '--merge exits 1 on a clean round' defect.
suggestion: Word the exit-1 condition as 'skipped > 0 and parsed == 0' so an empty input is explicitly clean, and add a test line under §10.5 item 32 asserting that a zero-byte role file merges with exit 0 while a file whose every non-empty line is malformed exits 1.

finding: Test 5 — 'Role units run concurrently and every other kind does not overlap them' — has no pinned observable. Comparing wall-clock start/end timestamps recorded by the fake runner is inherently racy: on a loaded machine two genuinely concurrent children can serialize, so the test flakes in the direction of a false failure, and a fast serial implementation can pass by accident. The spec gives the fake runner scripted exit codes but no rendezvous mechanism.
suggestion: Pin the observable: have the seam runner create a marker file and block until it sees its sibling's marker (with a timeout), so overlap is proven by both markers existing rather than by timestamps, and a serial implementation deadlocks the timeout deterministically.

finding: §10.6 asserts 'no other command's exit codes change outside `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, which no current test sets.' §8a changes `tp review --merge` and `tp audit --merge` from always exiting 0 on malformed input to exiting 1 when an input's lines all fail to parse — a command-level exit-code change outside TP_UNATTENDED, and existing merge tests that feed partially malformed fixtures and assert exit 0 are invalidated by it. The section that exists to enumerate invalidated tests contradicts §8a.
suggestion: Add the merge exit-code change to §10.6's list (name the merge tests that assert exit 0 on unparseable input) and soften the blanket claim to name the two commands whose exit codes change.

finding: The baseline file carries `spec_hash`, and §6.2 requires the Stop hook — a separate program shipped in the plugin — to evaluate the delta predicates 'against $TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-baseline.json'. The hash function, the file it is computed over, and any normalization (trailing newline, CRLF, whether the whole file or only the reviewed sections) are never stated, so the hook cannot reproduce a comparable value unless it shells out to some tp command that is also unnamed. `task_count` is likewise undefined (all tasks, or non-done tasks — which decides whether `decompose` succeeds when import replaces rather than adds).
suggestion: Name the digest and its input (e.g. SHA-256 over the spec file's raw bytes, the same value tp already stores as spec_hash) and define task_count as the total number of task entries. Better: give the hook a single command (e.g. `tp run --check-durable`) that evaluates the predicate, so driver and hook share one implementation instead of two.

finding: The per-attempt baseline file is specified as `{head_sha, spec_hash, task_count, round}` and written at spawn for EVERY unit, but (a) `round` is read by no predicate in §3.3 — both record kinds test "a round file for `$TP_ROUND` exists", which reads the env var, not the baseline — and (b) each of the other three fields is consumed by exactly one kind (`head_sha` by `audit-fix`, `spec_hash` by `review-resolve`, `task_count` by `decompose`), while `review-role`/`audit-role`/`review-record`/`audit-record`/`implement` have purely absolute predicates and measure nothing against a baseline. So the driver writes a file per attempt that five of eight kinds never open, and one field nothing opens at all.
suggestion: Drop `round` from the baseline (or drop `TP_ROUND` from the child env and make the record predicates read the baseline — one of the two is unearned), and write the baseline only for the kinds whose §3.3 predicate is a delta, stating in §3.1 that absolute-predicate kinds get none.

finding: `TP_FILE` was introduced as 'the resolved task file, so a child works the same target the driver resolved rather than re-running discovery', but no section defines how tp consumes it: which commands honour it, where it sits relative to a `--file` flag and the `.tp/local.json` active pointer, and what happens when it names a file that no longer exists. tp's discovery order is a documented contract, and this adds a layer to it inside §3.1's environment paragraph without touching §7 or the discovery documentation §8 lists. §10 has no test for it either, so the one variable the whole fresh-process model depends on for targeting is untested.
suggestion: Define TP_FILE's place in the discovery order (most naturally: below an explicit --file flag, above the active pointer), state it as a behaviour change of every file-resolving command in §8's documentation list, and add a §10.2 test that a child with TP_FILE set writes the driver's target even when the active pointer names another base.

finding: Spend reading is defined only for the success path: 'reads one number from the final line of that unit's log'. Nothing says what happens when the final line is not JSON, the spend_key path is absent, or the value is not a number — all routine for a runner that was killed by its own budget flag or crashed mid-stream. A test for a killed unit cannot assert whether spend is null, the unit is a failed attempt, or the run aborts.
suggestion: State that an unreadable or missing spend key yields spend null for that unit, is reported once on stderr, and never changes the unit's success/failure verdict (which is the exit code alone); add that case alongside test 11.

finding: §3.2.2 defines spend only for a runner that declares no spend_key (null, cap inert). It says nothing about a runner that declares one whose log is missing, empty, whose final line is not JSON, or lacks the key — the common case when a child is killed by its own --max-budget-usd or crashes mid-stream (§3.4 says such a unit 'exits non-zero and counts as a failed attempt', so its log will often be truncated). The implementer must guess whether spend_usd becomes null, whether cap-budget accrual silently under-counts, and whether the unresolvable read is itself an error.
suggestion: Specify: an unreadable or key-less final line records spend_usd null for that unit, contributes 0 to the accrued total, and is reported in --status (and at run start counted with the unmetered kinds) so a partial total is never mistaken for a complete one — the rule §3.2.2 already applies to unmetered runners.

finding: The `{max_budget_usd}` repair makes the placeholder resolve to a literal 0 for every template except `claude`, whose flag pair is dropped. But 0 is the spec's *disabled* sentinel (§7: 'run_max_unit_budget_usd | 0 (flag omitted)'), and a custom runner object with args like ['--budget','{max_budget_usd}'] will now receive '0' meaning, to most harnesses, 'spend nothing' — every unit aborts immediately at the default configuration. The repair made the placeholder always resolve at the cost of making the default value hostile to exactly the third-party runners §3.2 exists to support.
suggestion: Give the rule a sentinel-safe form: at 0 the driver drops the whole arg token containing the placeholder (which generalises the claude-template rule instead of special-casing it), or requires a runner object to declare `budget_arg` so the pair can be omitted the same way. If the literal must be passed, say in §7 that a custom runner is responsible for treating 0 as unlimited.

finding: Mixed per-kind accrual was pinned by making the run-start report name the unmetered kinds — but the run-start report is ephemeral stdout, while `.tp/run.json`'s `totals.spend_usd` (§3.5) and `tp run --status` ('spend against each cap') carry the partial total with no marker at all. The unattended operator reads the run *after* it stopped, which is exactly when the run-start line is gone, so the partial total is again mistakable for a complete one in both durable surfaces.
suggestion: Carry the marker where the number is read: add `unmetered_kinds[]` (or `spend_complete: false`) to `.tp/run.json`'s totals and to `--status`, and say it survives `--compact` alongside `stop_reason` and the cap totals per §7.

finding: Two run-start behaviours are required but have no test and no pinned form: 'run_max_budget_usd is inert for them — reported once at run start, not silently' and 'the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered'. Neither the channel (stdout, stderr, a run.json field, --status) nor the text or field name is given, and test 11 covers only that spend is null and cap-budget is inert.
suggestion: Pin the report as a named field (e.g. run start emits unmetered_kinds[] on stderr and in --status) and extend test 11 to assert the exact field for both the single-runner and per-kind-map cases.

finding: §3.2.2 promises that an unmetered runner's inertness is "reported once at run start, not silently", and that the per-kind report names which kinds are unmetered — but that promise covers `run_max_budget_usd` only. `run_max_unit_budget_usd` is equally inert for the `opencode` template (§3.2.1: no budget flag) and for any runner object whose `cmd` has no such flag, since §3.4 says the per-unit cap is "the runner's own flag, passed through rather than reimplemented". An operator who sets a per-unit dollar cap under `opencode` gets a knob that silently does nothing, which is the exact failure the run-start report exists to prevent.
suggestion: Extend the run-start report to name both budget fields when the resolved runner (or a kind in the per-kind map) supports neither a budget flag nor a `spend_key`, and say in §7 that `run_max_unit_budget_usd` applies only to runners declaring a budget flag.

finding: `audit-fix`'s new disjunct — 'the finding is recorded resolved without a change' — names a per-finding resolution record that exists for review (`tp review --resolve`/`--resolve-all`) but not for audit. Audit rounds are recorded as PASS/non-PASS result rows via `tp audit --record`; there is no audit artifact that marks an individual finding resolved, and §3.1 identifies an `audit-fix` unit only by 'the finding index'. The predicate therefore has no observable subject for the Stop hook (§6.2) or the driver to read, and Non-Goal 4/7 forbid inventing audit semantics here.
suggestion: Name the concrete artifact and how it is written, or restrict the disjunct to what audit already produces — e.g. 'HEAD differs from head_sha, or the unit wrote an escalation record' — and let a finding that needs no code change go through §5.2 rather than through a resolution record tp does not have.

finding: `review-role`/`audit-role` durable writes are existence-only ('the .ndjson exists'), so a role that emits a wholly unparseable file passes both the Stop hook and the driver's success test. §8a then makes `--merge` exit 1 for exactly that input — but the merge happens inside the *record* unit, one iteration later. §3.1's retry cleanup removes only the failed attempt's own files, so the record unit's retry re-reads the same bad role file and fails identically, and the run ends in `unit-failure` on a defect whose owner (the role unit) is never re-run.
suggestion: Either make the role predicate content-aware (the file exists and parses as NDJSON), or state in §3.3/§8a that a record unit failing on an unparseable input re-runs the offending role unit rather than retrying the record unit, and say which artifacts that removes.

finding: 'Caps are evaluated between iterations only... so a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration' names only two of the three counting caps. An iteration that spawns N concurrent role units also overshoots run_max_units, since cap-units fires on spawned children and the check happens after the iteration. As written, a test asserting 'no more than run_max_units children are ever spawned' is both derivable from the cap-units row and false under the evaluation rule.
suggestion: Add run_max_units to the overshoot sentence and state the bound explicitly (a single iteration may exceed run_max_units by up to the concurrent role count), then assert that bound rather than equality in test 3.

finding: The new in-flight/crashed rule pairs a single global `.tp/run.json` with a per-base lock: 'A run with no stop_reason reports in_flight when .tp/locks/run-<base>.lock is held and crashed when it is not.' §3.1 only forbids a second `tp run` over the *same* task file, so two runs over different bases are legal — they overwrite each other's `.tp/run.json`, and `--status` then probes whichever base it discovers rather than the base of the run recorded in the file. The result is a live run reported as `crashed`, or a crashed run reported as `in_flight`, from the one signal the spec calls 'the only evidence that separates the two'.
suggestion: Scope run state to the base as the lock already is (`.tp/run-<base>.json`), or record the base/lock path inside `.tp/run.json` and have `--status` probe that path rather than a rediscovered one; then say what `--status` reports when the recorded base differs from the discovered one.

finding: Two writers are described for the same file. §3.5 says the unit's runner output 'streams to $TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl' (the driver capturing stdout), while §3.2.1 passes `{log_path}` to the child as an argument and says the fake runner 'writes a final log line carrying that key'. If the driver redirects stdout to the path and the child also opens it, the two writes interleave or truncate each other and the spend read from 'the final line' is nondeterministic. The spec never says whether {log_path} is informational or a write target.
suggestion: Pick one owner: either the driver captures the child's stdout and {log_path} is passed only for the child's own reference (the fake runner then writes its spend line to stdout, not to the file), or the child owns the file and the driver never redirects. Say which, and say what happens if the child never creates the path.

finding: `last_failure` has two writers on two different paths — the driver, when a child exits non-zero, and tp itself, when a close fails its quality gate inside a child — plus a clearing rule keyed on `(unit_kind, unit_id)`. §3.5 mandates atomic temp+rename for `.tp/run.json` precisely because concurrent siblings write it, yet §4.2 states no atomicity, no lock, and does not say who evaluates the clear. With parallel role units a gate failure inside one child and a driver write for another can interleave on a file the spec says holds at most one object.
suggestion: Name the single writer (driver only, with gate output handed back through the child's exit path) or require the same atomic temp+rename plus a lock for `.tp/last_failure.json`, and state explicitly which component performs the `(unit_kind, unit_id)` clear.

finding: The fence covers review_max_rounds, audit_max_rounds, --skip-gate and import --force, but §7 adds run_max_units, run_max_wall_clock_seconds, run_max_budget_usd and run_max_unit_retries to the same `tp set --workflow` surface, and the spec never says when the driver resolves them. If caps are re-resolved each iteration (the natural reading of 'resolving at read time through the existing layered path'), an unattended unit can raise its own run's caps through a supported route — the exact hatch §5.1 exists to close. If they are resolved once at run start, an operator cannot lower a cap mid-run and the spec should say so.
suggestion: State that the driver resolves every run_* field once at run start and ignores later changes for the current run, and either add the run_* fields to §5.1's refusal table or state explicitly why raising them is harmless.

finding: §8a justifies the arity change by requiring that exit 2 mean 'usage error', so a driver can separate a mistyped invocation from a failed one without reading the message. §5.2 then gives exit 2 to `tp escalate`, an outcome it calls 'normal, expected... not a crash', and §5.1 gives exit 2 to policy refusals of well-formed commands. Under this spec exit 2 means at least three different things, and §5.2 has to add 'the record, not the exit code, is the signal' to work around its own overload — which is the ambiguity §8a says it is removing.
suggestion: State the reconciled meaning of exit 2 in one place: either narrow it back to malformed invocation and give escalation and unattended refusals their own code (e.g. 4, state), or drop §8a's 'without reading the message' claim and say the driver disambiguates exit 2 by the presence of an escalation record and a hint field.

finding: The driver exports `TP_FILE` so a child works the resolved target rather than re-discovering it, but nothing pins *which* `tp` executable the child invokes: §6.1's preflight compares `plugin.json`'s version against whatever `tp --version` PATH resolves to. During self-development CLAUDE.md requires every tp call to route through the freshly built binary, so a `tp run` launched from the dev binary would spawn children that call the lagging PATH release — the driver and its units then disagree about the very commands (`tp escalate`, `next_units`, `TP_ROUND_DIR` handling) this version adds, with no check that can detect the skew.
suggestion: Export the driver's own resolved executable path (e.g. `TP_BIN`) alongside `TP_FILE` and state that units invoke it, or require the driver to compare its own version against the PATH `tp` at run start and refuse to start on a mismatch.

finding: The PreToolUse deny lists '.tp-review/ contents, *.tasks.json, .tp/config.json and .tp/local.json' without saying how a tool's path argument is matched: whether the glob is basename-only (so vendor/other/foo.tasks.json is denied) or repo-root-anchored, whether relative and absolute paths and .. traversal are normalized first, and whether a path outside the repository is in scope. Test 25 asserts only that the four names are covered, so two engineers ship matchers that disagree on every nested or absolute path.
suggestion: State the matching rule once — resolve the tool's path to an absolute path, and deny when it is inside the repo root and matches any of the four patterns anchored at that root — and add the nested/absolute/traversal cases to test 25.

finding: The SessionStart hook's payload is fixed as `tp resume --compact` 'and nothing else', and §4.2 relies on `tp resume` surfacing `last_failure` to put the previous attempt's failure in front of the next unit. But the spec never says whether `--compact` preserves the two new resume fields (`next_units`, `last_failure`), and §7 specifies compact behaviour only for `tp run --status`. If `--compact` strips them on the same terms it strips per-unit rows, the single continuity mechanism the design claims a reset-native loop needs is silently absent from the only channel that delivers it.
suggestion: State in §4.1/§4.2 that `last_failure` and `next_units` survive `tp resume --compact` (and what is stripped instead), or change §6.2's payload to a form that carries them.

finding: Test 16 requires every §7 field to 'accept both range endpoints and reject one step outside each', but two of the seven rows have no endpoints: runner's Range is 'Built-in name or object' and notify_cmd's is 'Any command string'. The runner row is also narrower than §3.2, which allows a third shape (a per-kind map with a default key). A tester cannot derive the rejection cases for runner (unknown template name? map without default? non-object?) or for notify_cmd (empty string? whitespace-only?).
suggestion: Give runner an explicit validity rule in the table (built-in name from the fixed set, runner object, or per-kind map with default; a map missing default is exit 2) and say what an invalid notify_cmd is; scope test 16's endpoint clause to the five numeric fields and add a separate case for the two non-numeric ones.

finding: §3.2 says `runner` takes one of three shapes — built-in template name, runner object, or a per-kind map with a `default` key — and the per-kind map carries the section's main argument (running audit units on a different model). §7's table, which is the normative field/range surface that `tp config --resolved`, `--extract` and `tp validate --project` are said to cover, gives the range as 'Built-in name or object', omitting the map form entirely. A validator written from §7 rejects the shape §3.2 requires.
suggestion: Extend §7's range cell to 'Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map with `default`' and note that a map missing `default` is a usage error, so the validation surface matches §3.2.

finding: The merge payload gains `inputs` — one entry per input file `{path, parsed, skipped}` — emitted unconditionally on both `tp review --merge` and `tp audit --merge`. In the overwhelmingly common all-clean case every entry is `skipped: 0` and carries no information the exit code does not, yet a 5-role review pays five objects with full paths on every round, and a 4-role audit four. No `--compact` rule covers it either: §7's compact sentence ("`stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped") is scoped to run state, so nothing strips §8a's two new payloads.
suggestion: Emit `inputs` entries only for files with `skipped > 0`, alongside a scalar pair (`inputs_parsed`, `inputs_skipped`) that is always present — the exit-1-on-fully-unparsed rule is unaffected — and extend the `--compact` rule to §8a's additions explicitly.

finding: The section opens 'Four measured defects in the signals an unattended driver consumes … The measurements are in spec/0.35.0-candidates.md §1, §3, §7 and §10.' Round 4 added a fifth bolded item ('A dropped role does not merge clean') whose measurement is this spec's own round 4, not a candidates section, and neither the count nor the citation list was updated. It is a measured claim that the repair made false — the class CLAUDE.md flags as the cost of leaving stale numbers in a spec.
suggestion: Change the opening to five defects, and either add the new item's measurement to spec/0.35.0-candidates.md and cite it, or state inline that the fifth is measured on this spec's round 4 rather than in the candidates file.

finding: `location_clusters` is added to both `tp review --merge` and `tp review --status` while the same paragraph guarantees it changes no convergence arithmetic, no stored `clean` flag and no `--status --check` exit code — and test 28 pins exactly that. So it is a new array, emitted on the two payloads an unattended driver parses every round, that by construction feeds no decision the driver makes. The stated defect ("an unattended driver reads [duplicate locations] as rounds remaining") is not answered by an advisory array the driver is told to ignore; it is answered only if something acts on it.
suggestion: Either name the decision it feeds and make it act (e.g. a scalar `clustered_locations` count the driver records in `.tp/run.json` or reports on a non-converged stop), or reduce the emission to that scalar plus the per-location detail behind an explicit flag; and state that `--compact` strips it.

finding: location_clusters is given as {location, roles[], severities[], count} with no semantics for two of the four fields: count may be the number of findings at that location or the number of distinct roles, and severities[] may be a deduplicated set or one entry per finding, in an unspecified order. Cluster ordering is also unspecified, so a golden-JSON assertion is not reproducible. Test 28 asserts only that grouping happens, so it does not settle any of these.
suggestion: Pin count as the number of findings at the location, severities[] as the distinct severities in descending severity order, roles[] as distinct role ids sorted, and clusters sorted by location; assert the exact object in test 28.

finding: §8a's arity paragraph says every `Args` validator exits 2, 'matching §9's definition of a usage error'. §9 is Non-Goals — seven numbered items, none of which defines a usage error or mentions exit codes. The normative anchor for the change points at a section that cannot support it.
suggestion: Point the reference at the actual source of the exit-code contract (the tp exit-code table in skills/tp/REFERENCE.md, or state the definition inline in §8a: 2 = the invocation was malformed and nothing ran).

finding: Loop step 4 says 'units marked concurrent together', which reads as a per-unit marking the oracle supplies. §4.1 states the opposite: 'Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table', and `next_units` entries carry only `{kind, id, brief_command}`. A reader of §3.1 alone would look for a concurrency field that does not exist.
suggestion: Reword step 4 as 'Spawn a runner process per unit — kinds §3.3 marks parallel together, every other kind alone.'

finding: `TP_RUN_ID` is exported into every child's environment, but no child-side behaviour described anywhere in the spec reads it: artifacts anchor on `TP_RUN_DIR`/`TP_ROUND_DIR` (§3.1, §3.3, §5.2, §6.3), the Stop hook reads `TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_RUN_DIR` and `TP_UNIT_SEQ` (§6.2), and the only named `TP_RUN_ID` consumer is `notify_cmd`, which the driver spawns itself (§5.2). It is also mechanically derivable as the basename of `TP_RUN_DIR`, which the spec fixes as `.tp/runs/$TP_RUN_ID`.
suggestion: Either remove `TP_RUN_ID` from the child environment (keeping it for `notify_cmd`, whose consumer §5.2 names), or name the child-side consumer that justifies the ninth variable.

finding: `spend_key` is specified as a "dot path to the cost field", but every runner the spec defines uses a flat top-level key: `claude` reads `total_cost_usd`, the `TP_RUNNER` seam declares `total_cost_usd`, and `opencode` declares none. A dot-path grammar brings escaping and missing-segment questions (what a path into a non-object yields, whether a literal dot in a key can be expressed) that no shipped runner exercises, for a value the driver only ever reads once per unit.
suggestion: Specify `spend_key` as a top-level key name now, and note that nested-path support is added when a runner requires it — or, if the dot path stays, pin the failure behaviour for an unresolvable path (spend null, same as a runner declaring none) so it costs no extra decision.

finding: 'Test-only override' is a claim about intent with nothing enforcing it: TP_RUNNER is an ordinary environment variable, and the previous wording at least placed it inside a precedence an operator could reason about. As written, any environment that happens to export TP_RUNNER silently replaces the configured harness for a whole unattended run and outranks the operator's own CLI flag — the same class of silent substitution §5.1 spends a page arguing against.
suggestion: Say what makes it test-only (build tag, unexported test hook, or a documented guarantee that tp warns on stderr at run start when TP_RUNNER is honoured) or drop the adjective and treat it as a supported highest-precedence override with the reporting that implies.

finding: Test 15 (§10.2) and §10.6 require the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` to gain three entries covering `.tp/run.json`, `.tp/runs/` and `.tp/last_failure.json`, but the body only states that .tp/run.json (§3.5) and .tp/last_failure.json (§4.2) are git-ignored. `.tp/runs/` — which holds every log, baseline and escalation record — is never declared ignored outside the test list, so an implementer reading §3.5 alone ships a two-entry change and commits run logs.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §3.5 stating that `.tp/runs/` is git-ignored along with `.tp/run.json`, so the requirement lives in the body rather than only in the test list.

finding: last_failure is written 'when a unit exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate', but the second trigger fires inside tp done, which also runs interactively where no unit exists. The record's schema requires unit_kind, unit_id and phase, so a test for an interactive gate failure cannot say whether the file is written at all, or written with empty/absent unit fields — and whether it then blocks clearing by a later unit success, since clearing requires a (unit_kind, unit_id) match.
suggestion: Scope the gate trigger to a unit context: tp done writes last_failure only when TP_UNIT_KIND is set, and an interactive gate failure writes nothing. Add that negative case to test 23.

finding: `tp escalate` gains a repeatable `--option <text>` flag and the record gains `options[]`, but nothing in the spec ever reads them: the driver stops on the record's presence, `tp run --status` reports `stop_reason` (§3.5), `notify_cmd` receives only `TP_ESCALATION_PATH` (§5.2), and test 22 asserts only that the record is written. `evidence` already carries the free text the operator reads, so `options[]` is a second prose channel the agent must compose per escalation with no consumer and no rendering surface.
suggestion: Drop `--option`/`options[]` and let `evidence` carry the alternatives, or name where options are rendered (e.g. `tp run --status` on an escalation stop) so the bytes the unit spends produce something the operator actually sees.

finding: §7's `runner` row gives the range as 'Built-in name or object', but §3.2 defines a third accepted shape — a map from unit kind to a name or object, with a required `default` key. `tp validate --project` and `tp config --resolved` are required to cover the new fields 'on the same terms as every existing workflow field' (§7), so a validator written from the §7 table alone will reject the per-kind map that §3.2 calls the point of the abstraction.
suggestion: Extend the range cell to 'Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map with a required `default`', and state the validation error for a map missing `default` (usage error, exit 2) in §7 as well.
